justification: Judged as a Google policy reviewer against the current top results for 'process vs thread' / 'processes vs threads': ByteByteGo's guide and GeeksforGeeks' comparison page are exactly the low-value pattern the brief warns about — a short definitional intro, a bullet/table list of five or six differences, no runnable code, no measurements, no primary-source citations. This article is a different class of page: six original, verified C# programs (a shared-array vs. child-process demo, a 100-thread stack-footprint measurement, a crash-isolation demo, a context-switch relay benchmark, a creation-cost comparison across pool/thread/process, and a thread-pool-starvation demo), two labelled diagrams with real captions and accessible title/desc, four varied exercises with worked solutions, and 21 primary sources (Microsoft Learn, man7.org, dotnet/runtime, OSTEP, the Li/Ding/Shen USENIX paper, Chromium design docs) that are all cited inline. It clearly out-produces the best-ranking pages on value-add and originality, which is most of what this score is about. The self-reported timings (context-switch relay, per-thread stack cost, creation costs, pool starvation) are handled honestly: every number is qualified with a range, the machine's concurrent load is named as the cause of the wider-than-usual spread ('with other work sharing the machine while these numbers were taken', 'that run had more competition from other work on the machine'), and the text draws only the conclusions the ranges support ('two conclusions are safe...'). This is the opposite of fabricated precision and is a real strength. docs/crosslinks/operating-systems/processes-and-threads.md exists, lists sensible links with locations, and includes an explicit 'boundaries with planned siblings' section that scopes this article away from near-duplicate coverage of the race-condition, scheduling, virtual-memory and async/await articles — so the missing in-body links to those unpublished siblings are correctly not penalized here. Headings, exercise titles and the opening paragraph are specific to this content and not copied from the two published siblings I compared them against (SQL Joins, The Four Pillars of OOP) — no boilerplate 'Introduction'/'Conclusion', no repeated 'Predict the...' exercise framing, no filler intro or summary-that-repeats-the-headings outro. What holds the score down is a real breach of the binding 'never copy or closely paraphrase' rule, found by spot-checking distinctive sentences against the cited primary sources (see issues): one sentence reproduces a distinctive Chromium rationale almost word for word without quotation marks, and two further passages reproduce the exact item order and near-synonym wording of enumerated lists from Microsoft Learn ('About Processes and Threads' and 'Context Switches') closely enough that they read as transcribed rather than written from understanding. None of this is wholesale scraping and the volume of affected text is small relative to the article, but it is exactly the kind of passage a policy reviewer is trained to flag, and it is fixable without touching the facts, the code or the measurements. That caps the score below the 8.5 'equal to MDN/Real Python with only nits' band even though the rest of the article would clear it comfortably.

issues.location: Section 'A crash takes the whole process, and stops at its edge', paragraph beginning "That asymmetry is the main engineering reason to pay for a process."
issues.problem: The clause "it is close to impossible to build a rendering engine that never crashes or hangs" is a near-verbatim reproduction of the Chromium multi-process design document's sentence "It's nearly impossible to build a rendering engine that never crashes or hangs" (only 'nearly' is swapped for 'close to'; every other word and the clause order are identical). It is presented as the writer's own paraphrase, with no quotation marks and no signal that this is the source's own wording, which is exactly what Hard Rule 4 ('Never copy or closely paraphrase... write from understanding') forbids.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either quote the phrase directly with quotation marks and attribute it explicitly to the Chromium design document, or rewrite the point in a genuinely different sentence structure (e.g. state the engineering conclusion first — 'a renderer that can crash is a given' — and only then explain why, instead of following the source's own clause order).

issues.location: Section 'What belongs to the process and what belongs to each thread', first paragraph, sentence beginning "A process has a virtual address space..."
issues.problem: The list "a virtual address space, executable code, open handles to system objects, a security context, a process identifier, environment variables, a priority class and at least one thread" reproduces Microsoft Learn's 'About Processes and Threads' sentence ("A process has a virtual address space, executable code, open handles to system objects, a security context, a unique process identifier, environment variables, a priority class, minimum and maximum working set sizes, and at least one thread of execution") in the same order with only two items trimmed and 'unique'/'of execution' dropped. This is transcription of the source's own enumeration, not synthesis in the writer's own words.
issues.fixLooksLike: Regroup the same facts under the writer's own organizing idea (e.g. split into 'identity' items vs. 'resource' items, or fold some into the sentence that follows about threads sharing them) instead of repeating the source's list in its own order and near-identical wording.

issues.location: Section 'What a context switch costs', first paragraph, sentence beginning "Windows documents the steps..."
issues.problem: The four clauses "save the context of the outgoing thread, put it at the back of the queue for its priority if it is still runnable, find the highest-priority queue that has a ready thread, restore that thread's context and resume it" mirror the exact 4-step order of Microsoft Learn's 'Context Switches' page ('Save the context...', 'If the thread remains in a ready state, place it at the end of the queue for its priority level', 'Find the highest priority queue that contains ready threads', 'Remove the thread at the head of the queue, restore its context, and resume execution') with a near-synonym substituted for almost every clause — a textbook patchwriting pattern rather than a claim restated from understanding.
issues.fixLooksLike: Describe the mechanism in a structure that isn't a clause-by-clause substitution of the source's numbered list — for example, fold it into the following paragraph's discussion of what triggers a switch, or lead with the outcome (which thread ends up running) before the bookkeeping, so the sentence isn't reconstructible by lining it up against the source's four bullets.
